title: Louis Gave: Is the US Going Through McCarthy Again?
summary: In an Unheard interview, Gavekal's Louis Gave argues the Jensen Huang affair looks like an orchestrated campaign by the US national security establishment — and that from Beijing's perspective, it can only read as McCarthyism all over again.
body:
On Unheard, host Freddy Gray asks Gavekal founder Louis Gave — an investment adviser based in Hong Kong who knows China and how big tech companies operate — to lay out the theories behind the fall of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. Within 24 hours, Huang stepped down after admitting one extramarital affair with a woman US officials suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset, then a second affair was revealed, and by some reports a third. He has, in Gray's words, fallen on his sword, full of contrition. Gave's answer is blunt: what matters is not only what happened, but how it will be read in Beijing.

The first question is timing. The revelations about Huang had apparently been known for some time — reported in Taiwanese media, rumoured for a while. Why did they suddenly surface now? And why did the second affair follow so fast on the first? It gave a lot of people the sense that it was somehow an orchestrated campaign, Gray says. Gave agrees — and adds that a third affair was also announced, which, he says, perhaps explains why Huang decided to resign: "If you've had three affairs, chances are there's a fourth, a fifth, or sixth."

Gave puts himself in Huang's shoes. Huang was born in Taiwan and raised in the United States, and Gave draws on a distinction he has made for years: Western societies are based on guilt — you mess up, you say sorry, you start again, Christian forgiveness. Eastern societies are based on shame — more cohesive, but if you lose face, you lose absolutely everything. The day-by-day revelations, he argues, were very clearly meant to damage Huang's image, to humiliate him and the people he loves most.

The original New York Times article, Gave notes, said the information came out of the US State Department — not the FBI, not the CIA. The State Department, he says, was angry about Nvidia selling chips into China and was in a massive fight with the Commerce Department over it. Gray raises the theory that the affair exposed a division inside the administration: the Lutnick camp, more relaxed about trade with China, versus the incoming chief of staff Stephen Miller, seen as the head of a more sceptical camp.

Gave rejects the Miller theory and goes back in time. First the spy balloon in early 2023 — hysteria whipped up over an unmanned helium balloon, even though China has 1,600 satellites that could take pictures far better; the balloon was shot down, studied, and there was nothing in it, but state visits were cancelled. Then, a week before Trump was due to meet Xi Jinping in Busan in September 2025, the US moved the number of sanctioned Chinese companies from roughly 1,000 to 20,000. Xi, Gave says, "had a cow" and cut off rare earths. When China said no more rare earths and no more magnets, Ford and GM said they would have to idle plants within two weeks. Trump, who had not realised the sanctions had been massively increased, dialled it back and directed that from now on nobody does or says anything about China without going through Stephen Miller. Selling some chips to China was broadly part of that deal — a deal people in the national security establishment were clearly unhappy about.

"I'm an investor. I'm in the business of figuring out what the perception is, what policy is going to be," Gave says. Ten days ago, Trump took "an absolute drubbing" in the midterms. Within three or four days, the directives he had clearly stated — nobody does anything on China without going through him or Miller — went out the window. Suddenly people were leaking to the New York Times and the Financial Times a story they had known about for a year but had not felt comfortable leaking while Trump was powerful. "Trump loses power and all of a sudden, these stories come out."

That, Gave argues, is why this matters. If you are Xi Jinping, you had an agreement with Trump back in September 2025, a good 12 to 15 months, and now that Trump has lost an election, the national security establishment is back on top — an establishment that believes far less in win-win and positive engagement, and very much believes, as Gave puts it, in a Joe McCarthy-like approach: "there's a red under every bed, and if he's not under the bed then he's naked on top of the bed."

The spy story itself, Gave says, does not add up. Xi ordered all Chinese companies to stop buying Nvidia chips more than a year ago, to wean China off Nvidia models and build its own. Right now, he says, there are 600,000 H200 Nvidia chips sitting in Hong Kong waiting for Beijing to authorise their move into China — an authorisation Xi is not giving. So the idea that China would send spies to buy chips that Nvidia obviously wants to sell, while Xi blocks them — "how does this make sense?" Unless Huang was selling plans and trade secrets, and, Gave stresses, there is absolutely no proof any of that happened. "All he's done is sell chips." The attorney general, the CIA and even the ranking Democrat have said there is no conclusive evidence that Alice Huang is a spy.

Now imagine you are Xi, Gave says. Whether Alice Huang is a spy or not, you know. Suppose she is not — suppose the attorney general, the FBI and others saying there is nothing proving she is a spy are right, and the only evidence is one leak from the State Department to the New York Times. Then you are watching the US publicly humiliate and essentially execute its most successful CEO of the past 20 years on a totally bogus story. "How do you not conclude, if you're Xi Jinping, that the US is going through a McCarthy thing again? It's exactly the same thing. It's Joe McCarthy all over again." The net effect, Gray adds, is that Chinese trust in the US will be damaged either way.

Concretely, Gave says, China will stockpile — more semiconductors, more energy, more food — preparing for a more contentious relationship. And the leverage runs the other way now: the Western world needs Chinese magnets and rare earths. If the West tries new restrictions, China may cut off magnets again, and this time it might not scale the cutback back. Ford, GM, Caterpillar — if Caterpillar doesn't get the magnets, it can't produce earth-moving equipment. The two economies remain massively integrated, and when tensions rise, "you just have to get more nervous."

The Democrats, Gave notes, are weighing in from the right: Hillary Clinton said in the last 24 hours that if the government knows an American citizen is a target of an espionage operation and has reason to believe he does not know, "then you owe it to him to tell him." Gave wonders whether she has more information than the attorney general, the FBI director and the CIA director — or is simply trying to score cheap political points. He thinks it is the latter. From Beijing's perspective, there is really only one issue on which Americans are broadly bipartisan: "Democrats and Republicans can't even agree on what a woman is, but they can agree together to hate China."

David Sacks, who works for the president on technology, has said openly on X that he doesn't think Alice Huang was a spy and that the whole thing was a hit job; Elon Musk has implied the same; from the left, Glenn Greenwald and others agree. But no one can name who is running the operation. The newspapers quoted sources in the State Department. Gave's guess: not middle-ranking busybodies, but someone very senior — perhaps even the most senior person at the State Department, someone with presidential aspirations, deeply embedded in the national security establishment, who needs to show that establishment he is a serious candidate and mark a difference with Trump, who has now become toxic even inside his own administration.

For Gave the investor, the key point is the precedent. "Looking at what's just happened to Jensen Huang, it feels to me like he's just been Jack Ma." Jack Ma, the Alibaba boss, essentially went missing for six months after criticising the Chinese government. The perception then was that if they could go after Jack Ma, they could go after anybody — and it changed the dynamic in the markets. "If they can go after Jensen Huang, they can go after anybody. That means the risk premium on stocks goes up. If my CEO somehow screws the wrong person, my share price can go down 40% in two weeks." That applies in particular to technology companies with links to China or customer bases there.

What should we watch? Not Nvidia sales volumes to China, Gave says — China has been trying to block those itself. Watch whether, in the coming weeks and months, the West attempts new legislation, tighter trade restrictions, more embargoes. If it does, China will respond by embargoing rare earths, "and that will be a big blow to global economic growth."

Gave ends with a challenge to the listener: if you had lived in the McCarthy era, and McCarthy had waved his list of communists, would you have believed him? "I would have believed Joe McCarthy. Like, back then I would have believed, in the spirit of the time, I would have believed Joe McCarthy. And if you think, okay, I would have believed Joe McCarthy, then ask yourself: are they pulling the same tricks on me again?" Gray closes by noting there are no definite conclusions — except perhaps one: "it's not a great episode for US-China relations."
